digest.component_or_area: test hardening / wiki render byte-equivalence oracle
propositions: The byte-equivalence oracle invokes a copied _legacy_convert subprocess for all 884 prepared corpus units, adding 884 redundant Pandoc process spawns (~33s runtime) because both production and legacy sides read the same mutable _PANDOC_TO constant, making the legacy oracle not independently verify landed output.

The copied legacy subprocess is coupled to production via shared conversion constants; when _PANDOC_TO changed to plain, both production and legacy digests mutated identically, proving the oracle does not independently validate byte identity as its contract claims.

The immutable expected-output fixture must record exact generating Pandoc version and platform-specific SHA-256 binary fingerprints for all supported platforms (darwin-arm64, linux-x86_64) to preserve the stated test contract while eliminating 884 legacy subprocesses.

Patchset 1 failed Ubuntu cells (Python 3.11/3.12/3.13) because the schema stored only the macOS arm64 binary fingerprint and rejected the Linux x86_64 Pandoc 3.6.1 binary hash (4715627586c5d9c732e8f5a6b6bb9e27c4216a76a7729e043b24374dedf8a1f0) against the generating macOS hash (94ebf1efbce3561379e8f25de3efe5aeabee64dc36dd8e8b9e96cf05b4195c52), treating platform-specific provenance as platform-independent.

Patchset 2 repairs the schema to retain the complete platform-keyed fingerprint map and selects the exact supported hash by stable platform/architecture key, while all 884 real production _convert/Pandoc calls remain on every per-change run and the immutable output replaces only the copied legacy subprocess.

The deterministic generator validates installed Pandoc version and binary fingerprint against the complete supported-platform map before conversion, regenerates the fixture byte-identically when Pandoc is pinned, and fails closed on unknown platform or hash mismatch.
